title: The Alphabet, Diphthongs, and Accent
summary: The twenty-eight letters, each with one sound and one sound only; the six diphthongs; how consonant groups are sounded; and the single rule of accent from which no word departs.

script.heading: The Esperanto Alphabet

notes: The letters q, w, x and y do not belong to the alphabet.

Six letters carry a diacritic: the circumflex of ĉ, ĝ, ĥ, ĵ, ŝ — called a 'hat' by Esperantists — and the breve of ŭ. Older texts, and this course's source, write these as cx, gx, hx, jx, sx, ux where the letters cannot be printed.
There is not one letter with two sounds, nor one sound with two spellings. Learn the table and you can pronounce any word in the language on sight, and spell any word you hear.

rules.heading: The Alphabet
rules.statement: The Esperanto alphabet contains **twenty-eight** letters: a, b, c, ĉ, d, e, f, g, ĝ, h, ĥ, i, j, ĵ, k, l, m, n, o, p, r, s, ŝ, t, u, ŭ, v, z. The Latin letters **q, w, x** and **y** are not used, and six letters are added by means of a diacritical mark. The design is deliberate: the alphabet was fitted to the sounds of the language rather than inherited from another one, so that **each letter has one sound, and each sound one letter**.

examples.note: spelled bo, i, ro, do, o

rules.heading: The Vowels
rules.statement: There are **five vowels**, *a, e, i, o, u*, and each keeps one value wherever it stands, whether accented or not. English speakers must take particular care with **e** and **o**: the English vowels of "fate" and "toll" end in a slight vanish — a brief terminal *i* or *u* sound that makes them faintly diphthongal — and **no Esperanto vowel may be given such a vanish**.

examples.note: o-be-i; the final i is a full vowel

rules.heading: Consonants Differing from English
rules.statement: The consonants **b, d, f, h, k, l, m, n, p, t, v, z** have their English values. Of the remaining eleven, these need attention: **c** is always /ts/; **ĉ** is *ch* as in "chin"; **g** is always hard; **ĝ** is the *g* of "gem"; **ĥ** is the rasped *ch* of "loch"; **j** is the *y* of "yes"; **ĵ** is the *z* of "azure"; **ŝ** is *sh*; **r** is slightly trilled; **s** is always voiceless, never the /z/ of English "rose".

examples.note: the s-sound is absent; z is written where /z/ is meant

footnotes: Only a few words contain ĥ, and several of them are now more often written with k: ĥemio or kemio, chemistry.

rules.heading: The Names of the Letters
rules.statement: The vowels are named by their sounds. Each consonant is named by adding **-o**: *bo, co, ĉo, do, fo, go, ĝo, ho, ĥo, jo, ĵo, ko, lo, mo, no, po, ro, so, ŝo, to, ŭo, vo, zo*. These names are used in spelling words aloud and in reading abbreviations.

rules.heading: Diphthongs
rules.statement: A diphthong is two vowels uttered as a single sound, by one breath-impulse. Every Esperanto diphthong has **i** or **u** as its second element — but so that they may never be confused with two vowels that merely stand side by side, the second element is written **j** or **ŭ** and not *i* or *u*. Hence *naiva*, naive, has three syllables, while *najbaro*, neighbour, has three of a quite different shape.

paradigms.caption: The six diphthongs
paradigms.footnote: ŭ occurs only as the second element of a diphthong, never alone.

examples.note: na-I-va: ai here is **not** a diphthong, which is why the diphthong is written aj

rules.heading: Combinations of Consonants
rules.statement: Every consonant in a group is pronounced with its **full value**, whether the group stands at the beginning of a word or within it. **There are no silent letters.** English habits must therefore be resisted in four places: *kn, kv, gv, sv* sound both consonants; **kz** is not reduced to the *gz* or *ks* that English writes *x*; **sc** is the *sts* of "laST Said" said quickly; and **ng** keeps its *g*, as in "linger", not as in "singer". Two like letters together are each sounded, as in "inter-relate".

rules.heading: Syllables
rules.statement: A word contains **as many syllables as it has vowels and diphthongs** — a diphthong counting as one. The division is made thus: a single consonant goes with the vowel following it; a consonant followed by *l* or *r* goes with the *l* or *r*; otherwise the division falls before the last consonant of the group; and prefixes and the parts of compound words are kept whole.

examples.note: the b goes with the l
division before the last consonant of the group
the prefix mal- is kept whole

rules.heading: Accent
rules.statement: Words of more than one syllable are accented on **the syllable before the last**, without exception. Because the rule admits of none, the accent is never written; and because a diphthong is one syllable (¶7), counting the syllables correctly is the whole of the work.

examples.note: aŭ is one syllable, and it is the last; the accent falls on di

footnotes: Compare the languages Esperanto was meant to spare its learners: in Lithuanian, Russian or English the place of the accent must be memorised with each word.

drills.stem: How many letters are there in the Esperanto alphabet?
drills.explanation: Twenty-eight. The Latin alphabet loses q, w, x and y, and gains ĉ, ĝ, ĥ, ĵ, ŝ and ŭ.

drills.stem: Which of these letters does **not** belong to the Esperanto alphabet?
drills.explanation: q, w, x and y were left out. The sound English writes with y is written j.
ĉ is the *ch* of "chin". 'sh' is ŝ, and /ts/ is c.

drills.stem: Which statements about the Esperanto vowels are correct?
options: Each keeps one value whether accented or not.
**e** and **o** end in a slight vanish, as the English vowels of 'day' and 'go' do.
They are named by their own sounds.
drills.explanation: a, e, i, o, u, each with a single invariable value. The vanish of English "day" and "go" is exactly what must be avoided: Esperanto *e* is the vowel of "fiancé", not of "fate".
c is invariably /ts/, whatever vowel follows. /tʃ/ is written ĉ, and there is no letter with two values.
aj and aŭ are two of the six. *sc* and *kv* are consonant groups, each consonant of which is fully sounded (¶6).

drills.stem: Which syllable of **agrabla** ('agreeable') carries the accent?
options: none — the word is too short to be accented
drills.explanation: The word divides a-gra-bla, and the accent falls on the syllable before the last: a-GRA-bla. Note that *br* would not divide, the consonant before *l* or *r* going with it (¶7).

drills.stem: How many syllables are there in **samideano** ('fellow-believer')?
drills.explanation: Five: sa-mi-de-a-no. The *e* and *a* stand side by side but do not form a diphthong — a diphthong would be written *aj* or *aŭ* (¶5) — so each is a syllable of its own.

drills.stem: How is the group **sc** pronounced in *scias* ('knows')?
options: as /sts/, both letters keeping their full value
drills.explanation: c is /ts/ everywhere, so *sc* is /sts/ — the sound of "laST Said" run together. Nothing is ever silent in Esperanto.

drills.stem: Which statements about the Esperanto accent are correct?
options: It falls on the syllable before the last, in every word of more than one syllable.
It is written with an acute accent in ordinary text.
A diphthong counts as a single syllable when the place of the accent is worked out.
It never has to be learned word by word.
drills.explanation: The rule has no exceptions, so nothing needs marking and nothing needs memorising — the whole difficulty is counting syllables, and there a diphthong counts as one. In *hodiaŭ*, *aŭ* is the last syllable and *di* takes the accent.

drills.stem: How many syllables are there in **ĉielo** ('sky, heaven')?
drills.explanation: Three: ĉi-e-lo, hence ĉi-E-lo. *ie* is not a diphthong — the diphthongs all end in j or ŭ — so the i and the e are separate syllables.

options: as the ng of 'singer', a single nasal sound
as the ng of 'linger', the g being distinctly heard
as /n/, the g being silent before v
drills.explanation: Each consonant of a group keeps its full value, so the g is sounded — "linger", not "singer". A silent letter does not exist in the language.
